questions.question: A tap fills a cistern in 14 hours. Another tap empties the full tank in 18 hours. How long (in hours) will it take to fill the tank completely, if the tank is empty and both the taps are open together?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Net filling rate = (**A × B**) ÷ (**B − A**) where **A** is filling time and **B** is emptying time.

Time taken = (**14 × 18**) ÷ (**18 − 14**)

Time taken = (**14 × 18**) ÷ **4** = **252 ÷ 4**

Time taken = **63 hours**.

**∴ The correct answer is 63 hours.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Filling tap time = **14 hours**, Emptying tap time = **18 hours**.

 
 **Tap Type** **Hours** **Total Work (LCM)** **Efficiency** 
 Filling Tap (A) 14 126 units +9 
 Emptying Tap (B) 18 −7 

⇒ Net efficiency of both taps = **9 − 7** = **2 units/hour**

⇒ Total work to fill the tank = **126 units**

⇒ Time taken = **Total Work ÷ Net Efficiency**

⇒ Time taken = **126 ÷ 2**

⇒ Time taken = **63 hours**

**∴ The correct answer is 63 hours.**

**__Additional Information__**

Pipes and Cisterns Concept

Filling taps have **positive efficiency**, while emptying taps (leakage) have **negative efficiency**.

Net Work Formula

If pipe A fills in 'x' hours and pipe B empties in 'y' hours (where y > x), time to fill is **xy/(y − x)**.

LCM Method

Total capacity is assumed as the **LCM** of individual times to simplify unit-based calculations.</p

questions.question: A can complete a piece of work in 24 days and B can complete it in 28 days. If they work on alternate days, starting with B on the first day, then in how many days will the work be finished?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Total Work (LCM of 24, 28) = **168 units**.

Efficiency: **A = 7**, **B = 6**.

2-day work cycle (B then A) = 6 + 7 = **13 units**.

In 12 cycles (24 days), work done = 12 × 13 = **156 units**. Remaining = 12 units.

Day 25 (B's turn): B does 6 units. Remaining = 6 units. Day 26: A takes 6/7 days.

**∴ The correct answer is 25 6/7 days.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Time taken by **A** = 24 days, **B** = 28 days. Working **alternately** starting with **B**.

**Formula Used:** Efficiency = Total Work ÷ Time; Total Work = LCM of individual times.

 
 **Person** **Days** **Total Work** **Efficiency** 
 **A** 24 168 7 
 **B** 28 6 

⇒ Total efficiency in a 2-day cycle (B + A) = 6 + 7 = 13 units.

⇒ Number of complete cycles = 168 ÷ 13 = 12 cycles with a remainder.

⇒ Work completed in 12 cycles (24 days) = 12 × 13 = 156 units.

⇒ Remaining work = 168 − 156 = 12 units.

⇒ On 25th day, **B** works and completes 6 units. Remaining = 12 − 6 = 6 units.

⇒ On 26th day, **A** works. Time taken by A = Remaining work ÷ Efficiency = 6 ÷ 7 days.

⇒ Total time = 24 + 1 + 6/7 = 25 6/7 days.

**∴ The correct answer is 25 6/7 days.**

**__Additional Information__**

Alternate Day Work

In alternate day problems, identify the **unit cycle** (usually 2 days) and calculate work per cycle. The starting person significantly affects the remainder calculation.

Time and Work Relation

Work is always considered as 1 unit or the **LCM** of given days to simplify calculations. Efficiency is **inversely proportional** to time taken.</p

questions.question: A tap fills a cistern in 9 hours. Another tap empties the full tank in 90 hours. How long (in hours) will it take to fill twice the volume of the tank, if the tank is empty initially and both the taps are open together?
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Net efficiency = 1/9 − 1/90 = (10 − 1)/90 = 9/90 = 1/10 per hour.

Time to fill one tank = 10 hours.

Time to fill **twice the volume** = 10 × 2 = 20 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 20 hours.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Filling tap time = 9 hours, Emptying tap time = 90 hours.

**Formula Used:** Total Work = LCM of time | Efficiency = Total Work ÷ Time

 
 **Person** **Hours** **Total Work** **Efficiency** 
 Filling Tap 9 90 units +10 
 Emptying Tap 90 −1 

⇒ Combined efficiency = 10 − 1 = 9 units/hour

⇒ Capacity of tank = 90 units

⇒ Target volume (twice) = 90 × 2 = 180 units

⇒ Time required = 180 ÷ 9 = 20 hours

**∴ The correct answer is 20 hours.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Inlet and Outlet Taps

Inlet pipes have positive efficiency as they add water, while outlet/leakage pipes have negative efficiency as they remove water.

Net Work Done

If two pipes fill and empty at rates 'a' and 'b', the net rate is (1/a − 1/b) per unit time.

Volume Scaling

If the volume to be filled is multiplied by a factor 'k', the total time taken also scales by 'k' assuming constant rates.</p

questions.question: A cistern has a hole in the bottom through which the water is leaking. A tap can fill the cistern in 6 hours and the hole in the bottom can empty the fully filled cistern in 15 hours. If both the tap and the hole are open, then what will be the time taken to completely fill the empty cistern?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Net filling time = (**a × b**) ÷ (**b − a**), where a = filling time and b = emptying time.

Net filling time = (**6 × 15**) ÷ (**15 − 6**)

Net filling time = **90 ÷ 9** = **10 hours**.

**∴ The correct answer is 10 hr.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Time taken by **Tap (A)** to fill = **6 hours**

Time taken by **Hole (B)** to empty = **15 hours**

 **Source**
 **Time (hr)**
 **Total Capacity (LCM)**
 **Efficiency**

 **Tap (A)**
 6
 30 units
 +5

 **Hole (B)**
 15
 −2

**Calculations:**

⇒ **Total Capacity** = LCM(6, 15) = **30 units**

⇒ **Efficiency of Tap (A)** = 30 ÷ 6 = **+5 units/hr**

⇒ **Efficiency of Hole (B)** = 30 ÷ 15 = **−2 units/hr**

⇒ **Combined Efficiency (A + B)** = 5 − 2 = **3 units/hr**

⇒ **Time taken to fill the cistern** = Total Capacity ÷ Combined Efficiency

⇒ **Time** = 30 ÷ 3 = **10 hours**

**∴ The correct answer is 10 hr.**

**__Additional Information__**

Inlet and Outlet Pipes

An **inlet pipe** fills the tank (positive efficiency), while an **outlet pipe** (or leak) empties the tank (negative efficiency).

Net Work Done

If 1/x is the filling rate and 1/y is the emptying rate, net work per hour = **1/x − 1/y** (when filling is faster).

Pipes & Cisterns Analogy

This concept is identical to **Time & Work**, where filling is **positive work** and emptying/leaking is **negative work**.</p

questions.question: Pipes A and B can fill an empty cistern in 21 minutes and 42 minutes, respectively. Both Pipe A and Pipe B are opened together. After how much time should Pipe B be turned off so that the empty cistern is completely filled in a total of 16 minutes?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Total Capacity (LCM of 21, 42) = 42 units.

Efficiency: A = 42/21 = 2 units/min; B = 42/42 = 1 unit/min.

Pipe A works for the full 16 minutes → 16 × 2 = 32 units.

Remaining work (to be done by B) = 42 − 32 = 10 units.

Time for Pipe B = 10 units ÷ 1 unit/min = 10 minutes.

**∴ The correct answer is 10 min.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Filling time for **Pipe A** = 21 minutes, **Pipe B** = 42 minutes. Total time for filling = 16 minutes.

**Formula Used:** Total Work = Efficiency × Time; Efficiency = 1 / Time taken to fill.

 
 **Person** **Days** **Total Work** **Efficiency** 
 Pipe A 21 min 42 units 2 units/min 
 Pipe B 42 min 1 unit/min 

⇒ Let Pipe B be turned off after **x** minutes.

⇒ Work done by Pipe A in 16 minutes + Work done by Pipe B in x minutes = 42

⇒ (Efficiency of A × 16) + (Efficiency of B × x) = 42

⇒ (2 × 16) + (1 × x) = 42

⇒ 32 + x = 42

⇒ x = 42 − 32 = 10 minutes.

**∴ The correct answer is 10 min.**

**__Additional Information__**

Pipes & Cisterns Efficiency

Efficiency is **inversely proportional** to the time taken. If a pipe fills a tank in 't' hours, its work done in 1 hour is 1/t.

Inlet and Outlet Pipes

Inlet pipes do **positive work** while outlet (leakage) pipes do **negative work**. Combined efficiency = Σ(Inlet Efficiency) − Σ(Outlet Efficiency).

LCM Method

Total capacity of the tank is assumed as the **LCM** of the individual times to simplify calculations into integers.</p

questions.question: A and B can complete a work in 11 days and 33 days, respectively. They started doing the work together, but after 3 days, B had to leave, and A completed the remaining work alone. The remaining work was completed in ______ days.
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

**Total Work** (LCM of 11, 33) = 33 units.

**Efficiency**: A = 3, B = 1. Combined efficiency = 4.

Work done in 3 days = 4 × 3 = 12 units.

Remaining work = 33 − 12 = 21 units.

Days taken by A alone = 21 ÷ 3 = 7 days.

**∴ The correct answer is 7 days.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Time taken by **A** = 11 days, Time taken by **B** = 33 days. Together they work for 3 days.

**Formula Used:** Total Work = Time × Efficiency; Efficiency = Work / Time.

 
 **Person** **Days** **Total Work** **Efficiency** 
 A 11 33 3 
 B 33 1 

⇒ **Combined Efficiency** (A + B) = 3 + 1 = 4 units/day.

⇒ Work completed by both in 3 days = 4 × 3 = 12 units.

⇒ **Remaining Work** = Total Work − Completed Work = 33 − 12 = 21 units.

⇒ Time taken by **A** to finish 21 units = 21 ÷ 3 = 7 days.

**∴ The correct answer is 7 days.**

**__Additional Information__**

Pipes & Cisterns

Similar to time and work, but use negative efficiency for outlet pipes that drain the tank.

Work & Wages

Wages are always distributed in the ratio of the actual work done or the ratio of efficiencies if they work for the same duration.

Chain Rule

Use the M₁D₁H₁/W₁ = M₂D₂H₂/W₂ formula for problems involving different groups of workers.</p

questions.question: A tap fills a cistern in 18 hours. Another tap empties the full tank in 19 hours. How long (in hours) will it take to fill one-third of the tank, if the tank is empty initially and both the taps are open together?
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Net efficiency for filling the tank = 1/18 − 1/19 = 1/342 part per hour.

Time to fill the **full tank** = 342 hours.

Time to fill **one-third** of the tank = 342 ÷ 3 = 114 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 114 hours.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

**Filling Tap** time = 18 hours

**Emptying Tap** time = 19 hours

**Target:** Fill 1/3 of the tank capacity.

 
 **Tap Type** **Time (hr)** **Total Work (LCM)** **Efficiency** 
 Inlet (+) 18 342 units +19 
 Outlet (−) 19 −18 

**Calculations:**

⇒ Total capacity of the cistern = **LCM**(18, 19) = 342 units.

⇒ Net efficiency of both taps = 19 − 18 = 1 unit/hour.

⇒ Target volume to be filled = 1/3 × 342 = 114 units.

⇒ Time required = Target Volume ÷ Net Efficiency

⇒ Time required = 114 ÷ 1 = 114 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 114 hours.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Pipes and Cisterns Basics

Efficiency of an **Inlet pipe** is always positive, while the efficiency of an **Outlet (leakage) pipe** is taken as negative.

Total Work Concept

Total capacity or work is usually the **Least Common Multiple (LCM)** of the individual times taken by each pipe.

Combined Rate Formula

If pipe A fills in 'x' hours and pipe B empties in 'y' hours, net rate per hour is (1/x − 1/y). Tank fills only if x < y.</p

questions.question: A can complete a piece of work in 14 days and B can complete it in 10 days. If they work on alternate days, starting with B on the first day, then in how many days will the work be finished?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

**Total Work** (LCM of 14, 10) = 70 units.

Efficiency: **A** = 5, **B** = 7. **2-day cycle** (B + A) = 7 + 5 = 12 units.

5 cycles (10 days) = 12 × 5 = 60 units. Remaining = 70 − 60 = 10 units.

Day 11 (B's turn) = 7 units. Remaining = 10 − 7 = 3 units.

Day 12 (A's turn) takes 3 ÷ 5 = 3/5 day.

**∴ The correct answer is 11 3/5 days.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Time taken by **A** = 14 days, Time taken by **B** = 10 days.

 
 **Person** **Days** **Total Work** **Efficiency** 
 **A** 14 70 5 
 **B** 10 7 

⇒ Total work = **LCM**(14, 10) = 70 units.

⇒ Efficiency of **A** = 70 ÷ 14 = 5 units/day.

⇒ Efficiency of **B** = 70 ÷ 10 = 7 units/day.

⇒ Work done in first **2 days** (B then A) = 7 + 5 = 12 units.

⇒ In 10 days (5 cycles), work completed = 12 × 5 = 60 units.

⇒ Remaining work = 70 − 60 = 10 units.

⇒ On **11th day**, **B** works and completes 7 units. Remaining = 10 − 7 = 3 units.

⇒ On **12th day**, **A** works. Time taken = 3/5 days.

⇒ Total time = 10 + 1 + 3/5 = 11 3/5 days.

**∴ The correct answer is 11 3/5 days.**

**__Additional Information__**

Alternate Day Work

When individuals work alternately, calculate the combined work of one full cycle and multiply to get as close to the total work as possible without exceeding it.

Efficiency and Time

Efficiency is inversely proportional to time. Total Work = Efficiency × Time. Using LCM for total work simplifies fractional calculations.</p

questions.question: A tap fills a cistern in 18 hours. Another tap empties the full tank in 24 hours. How long (in hours) will it take to fill three-fourth of the tank, if the tank is empty initially and both the taps are open together?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Net efficiency = Fill rate − Empty rate = 1/18 − 1/24 = (4 − 3)/72 = 1/72 unit/hr.

Time to fill full tank = 72 hours.

Time to fill 3/4th tank = 72 × 3/4 = 18 × 3 = 54 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 54 hours.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Filling Tap **(A)** = 18 hours, Emptying Tap **(B)** = 24 hours.

**Formula Used:** Total Work = LCM of time; Efficiency = Work ÷ Time.

 
 **Tap** **Time (hrs)** **Total Work (LCM)** **Efficiency** 
 A (Fill) 18 72 units +4 
 B (Empty) 24 −3 

⇒ Combined Efficiency of (A + B) = 4 − 3 = 1 unit/hr

⇒ Target Work = 3/4 × Total Work = 3/4 × 72 = 54 units

⇒ Time Required = Target Work ÷ Combined Efficiency = 54 ÷ 1 = 54 hours

**∴ The correct answer is 54 hours.**

**__Additional Information__**

Net Work Done

When one pipe fills (x) and another empties (y), net work in 1 hour = (1/x − 1/y). If the result is positive, the tank fills; if negative, it empties.

Pipes and Cisterns vs Time and Work

The logic is identical to **Time and Work**, but the **emptying tap** (outlet) is treated as having **negative efficiency**.

Partial Filling

To find time for a fraction (k) of the tank, use: Time = (k × Total Capacity) ÷ Net Efficiency.</p

questions.question: A cistern has a hole in the bottom through which the water is leaking. A tap can fill the cistern in 8 hours and the hole in the bottom can empty the fully filled cistern in 10 hours. If both the tap and the hole are open, then what will be the time taken to completely fill the empty cistern?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__
Time taken by **Filling Tap** (A) = 8 hours

Time taken by **Emptying Hole** (B) = 10 hours

Combined Time = (A × B) ÷ (B − A)

Net Time = (8 × 10) ÷ (10 − 8) = 80 ÷ 2 = 40 hours

**∴ The correct answer is 40 hr.**

**__Alternate Method__**

 **Pipe/Hole** **Time (hr)** **Total Work (LCM)** **Efficiency**
 Filling Tap (+) 8 40 +5
 Emptying Hole (−) 10 −4
**Given:** Filling time = 8 hr, Emptying time = 10 hr.

**Formula:** Total Work = LCM(8, 10) = 40 units.

⇒ Efficiency of **Filling Tap** = 40 ÷ 8 = +5 units/hr

⇒ Efficiency of **Emptying Hole** = 40 ÷ 10 = −4 units/hr

⇒ Combined Efficiency = 5 − 4 = +1 unit/hr

⇒ Time taken to fill = Total Work ÷ Combined Efficiency = 40 ÷ 1 = 40 hours

**∴ The correct answer is 40 hr.**

**__Additional Information__**

Net Efficiency Rule

When one pipe fills (rate x) and another empties (rate y), the net work done per hour is (1/x − 1/y) if x < y.

Pipes and Cisterns vs Time and Work

The concepts are identical, but in cisterns, work done by an **outlet/leak** is taken as **negative work**.</p

questions.question: A tap fills a cistern in 18 hours. Another tap empties the full tank in 24 hours. How long (in hours) will it take to fill one-fourth of the tank, if the tank is empty initially and both the taps are open together?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Net efficiency = 4 (fill) − 3 (empty) = 1 unit/hour.

Total Capacity (LCM of 18, 24) = 72 units.

One-fourth of the tank = 72 ÷ 4 = 18 units.

Time taken = 18 units ÷ 1 unit/hour = 18 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 18 hours.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Filling Tap (A) time = 18 hours, Emptying Tap (B) time = 24 hours.

**Formula Used:** Efficiency = Total Work ÷ Time; Required Time = Required Work ÷ Net Efficiency.

⇒ Net efficiency when both open = 4 + (−3) = 1 unit/hour.

⇒ Work to be done = 1/4 × Total Capacity = 1/4 × 72 = 18 units.

⇒ Time required = 18 ÷ 1 = 18 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 18 hours.**

**__Additional Information__**

Net Work Done

When one pipe fills and another empties, net work per hour = (1/x − 1/y), where x is filling time and y is emptying time.

LCM Method

Always assume total capacity as the LCM of individual times to avoid working with complex fractions.

Inlet and Outlet Pipes

Inlet pipes have positive efficiency (+), whereas outlet/leakage pipes have negative efficiency (−).</p

questions.question: A cistern has a hole in the bottom through which the water is leaking. A tap can fill the cistern in 8 hours and the hole in the bottom can empty the fully filled cistern in 12 hours. If both the tap and the hole are open, then what will be the time taken to completely fill the empty cistern?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Net work done per hour = (1 ÷ **Filling time**) − (1 ÷ **Emptying time**)

Net filling rate = (1 ÷ 8) − (1 ÷ 12) = (3 − 2) ÷ 24 = 1 ÷ 24

Total time taken = 24 hours

**∴ The correct answer is 24 hr.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Time taken by **Tap** (Inlet) = 8 hours

Time taken by **Hole** (Outlet) = 12 hours

 **Source**
 **Time (hr)**
 **Total Work (LCM)**
 **Efficiency**

 **Tap**
 8
 24 units
 +3

 **Hole**
 12
 −2

**Calculations:**

⇒ Total Capacity (LCM of 8 and 12) = 24 units

⇒ Net efficiency (when both open) = 3 − 2 = 1 unit/hr

⇒ Time required = Total Capacity ÷ Net Efficiency

⇒ Time required = 24 ÷ 1 = 24 hours

**∴ The correct answer is 24 hr.**

**__Additional Information__**

Net Rate Formula

When one pipe fills (x) and another empties (y), the time taken (T) is given by 1/T = 1/x − 1/y, provided x < y.

Pipes and Cisterns Logic

Inlet pipe efficiency is taken as **positive** (+) and outlet/leak efficiency is taken as **negative** (−).

Efficiency and Time

Efficiency is **inversely proportional** to the time taken to complete the work.</p

questions.question: A water tank can be filled in 48 minutes by using 4 pipes of the same capacity. In how many minutes (rounded off to two decimal places) will the water tank be filled if we use 26 pipes of the same capacity as above?
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__
Apply **Inverse Proportion** formula: **M₁D₁ = M₂D₂**

4 pipes × 48 minutes = 26 pipes × **Time**

Time = (4 × 48) ÷ 26 = 192 ÷ 26

Time ≈ 7.38 minutes

**∴ The correct answer is 7.38 minutes.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Initial number of **pipes** (n₁) = 4

Initial **time taken** (t₁) = 48 minutes

Final number of **pipes** (n₂) = 26

**Formula Used:**

For constant work, **Number of Pipes** is **Inversely Proportional** to **Time Taken**.

n₁ × t₁ = n₂ × t₂

**Calculations:**

⇒ 4 × 48 = 26 × t₂

⇒ 192 = 26 × t₂

⇒ t₂ = 192 ÷ 26

⇒ t₂ = 96 ÷ 13

⇒ t₂ ≈ 7.3846...

⇒ t₂ ≈ 7.38 minutes (rounded off to two decimal places)

**∴ The correct answer is 7.38 minutes.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Inverse Proportion

When one quantity increases and the other decreases at the same rate, it is called inverse variation (x₁y₁ = x₂y₂).

Pipes and Cisterns Logic

More pipes of the same capacity will fill the tank in less time. Total capacity = Number of pipes × Time × Efficiency per pipe.

Rounding Off Rule

If the third decimal digit is 5 or greater, round up the second digit; otherwise, keep the second digit as is.</p

questions.question: Two taps can fill a cistern in 2 hours and 81 hours, respectively. A third tap can empty it in 81 hours. How long (in hours) will it take to fill the empty cistern, if all of the taps are opened together?

Pipes and Cisterns Efficiency

Net Rate of Filling

Total Work Concept

questions.question: A tap fills a cistern in 15 hours. Another tap empties the full tank in 17 hours. How long (in hours) will it take to fill two-third of the tank, if the tank is empty initially and both the taps are open together?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Net efficiency = 1/15 − 1/17 = (17 − 15) / 255 = 2 / 255 cistern/hour.

Time for full tank = 255 / 2 hours.

Time for 2/3rd tank = (255 / 2) × (2 / 3) = 255 / 3 = 85 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 85 hours.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Filling Tap (A) = 15 hours, Emptying Tap (B) = 17 hours.

**Formula Used:** Efficiency = Total Work ÷ Time

 
 **Tap** **Time (hr)** **Total Capacity (LCM)** **Efficiency** 
 Tap A (+) 15 255 units +17 
 Tap B (−) 17 −15 

⇒ Combined efficiency of (A + B) = 17 − 15 = 2 units/hour.

⇒ Required filling volume = 2/3 × 255 units = 2 × 85 = 170 units.

⇒ Time required = Required volume ÷ Combined efficiency

⇒ Time = 170 ÷ 2 = 85 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 85 hours.**

**__Additional Information__**

Pipes and Cisterns Efficiency

Filling pipes have **positive efficiency** while emptying pipes (leakages) have **negative efficiency**.

Net Rate Formula

If a pipe fills in 'x' hours and another empties in 'y' hours, net time to fill is (xy) ÷ (y − x) where y > x.

Fractional Work

Total time to fill a specific fraction 'k' of the tank is k × (Total time for full tank).</p

questions.question: A water tank can be filled in 38 minutes by using 44 pipes of the same capacity. In how many minutes (rounded off to two decimal places) will the water tank be filled if we use 37 pipes of the same capacity as above?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Total work = **Pipes × Time**

44 × 38 = 37 × Required Time

Required Time = (44 × 38) ÷ 37

Required Time = 1672 ÷ 37 ≈ 45.19

**∴ The correct answer is 45.19 minutes.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Number of initial pipes (M₁) = 44

Initial time taken (D₁) = 38 minutes

Number of final pipes (M₂) = 37

**Formula Used:**

M₁D₁ = M₂D₂

**Calculations:**

⇒ 44 × 38 = 37 × D₂

⇒ 1672 = 37 × D₂

⇒ D₂ = 1672 ÷ 37

⇒ D₂ = 45.1891...

⇒ D₂ ≈ 45.19 minutes

**∴ The correct answer is 45.19 minutes.**

**__Additional Information__**

Inverse Proportion

When the number of pipes increases, the time taken to fill the tank decreases, following the relation M₁T₁ = M₂T₂.

Pipes & Cisterns Efficiency

Total capacity is treated as constant work. Efficiency is directly proportional to the number of identical pipes used.</p

questions.question: An electric pump can fill a tank in 3 hours. Due to a leakage in the tank, it takes 5 (1/4) hours to fill the tank. How much time will this leak take to empty the full tank if water does not get in or out of the tank through any other point during this period?

Let filling time **A = 3 hours** and combined time (filling + leak) **B = 21/4 hours**.

Leak empty time = (A × B) ÷ (B − A)

⇒ (3 × 21/4) ÷ (21/4 − 3) = (63/4) ÷ (9/4) = 63 ÷ 9 = 7 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 7 hr.**

⇒ Efficiency of **Pump + Leak (P+L)** = 4 units/hr

questions.question: Nirbhay can complete a piece of work alone in 19 days and Vismay can complete the same piece of work alone in 6 days. They started the work together, but Nirbhay had to leave 4 days before the completion of the work. In how many days will the work get completed?

Trick: When someone leaves **before completion**, add their potential work for those days to the Total Work.

Total units = 114 + (6 × 4) = 114 + 24 = 138 units.

Total time = 138 ÷ (6 + 19) = 138 ÷ 25 = 5(13/25) days.

questions.question: A, B and C alone can do a piece of work in 11, 33 and 48 days, respectively. They all started the work together, but A left after 2 days. In how many days was the remaining work completed?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Total Work = LCM(11, 33, 48) = **528 units**.

Efficiencies: A = 48, B = 16, C = 11.

Work done by (A+B+C) in 2 days = (48 + 16 + 11) × 2 = 75 × 2 = **150 units**.

Remaining work = 528 − 150 = **378 units**.

Remaining time taken by (B+C) = 378 ÷ (16 + 11) = 378 ÷ 27 = **14 days**.

**∴ The correct answer is 14 days.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Time taken by A = 11 days, B = 33 days, C = 48 days.

**Formula Used:** Efficiency = Total Work ÷ Time; Work Done = Efficiency × Time.

 A 11 528 48 
 B 33 16 
 C 48 11 

⇒ Combined efficiency of A, B and C = 48 + 16 + 11 = 75 units/day.

⇒ Work completed in first 2 days = 75 × 2 = 150 units.

⇒ Remaining Work = 528 − 150 = 378 units.

⇒ Combined efficiency of B and C = 16 + 11 = 27 units/day.

⇒ Time taken by B and C to complete remaining work = 378 ÷ 27.

⇒ Time = 14 days.

**∴ The correct answer is 14 days.**

**__Additional Information__**

Combined Work Efficiency

When multiple people work together, their daily efficiencies are added. Combined Efficiency = E₁ + E₂ + ... + Eₙ.

Work Left Concept

If a person leaves after 'n' days, their contribution is calculated as (Efficiency × n) and subtracted from the total work to find the remainder.

Time and Work Relation

Total Work = Efficiency × Time. For a constant work, Efficiency is inversely proportional to Time.</p

questions.question: Nick, Kevin, and Joe can finish a certain piece of work in 3, 9, and 27 days respectively. All three of them started the work together. Total Work (LCM of 3, 9, 27) = 27 units.

Efficiencies: **Nick** = 9, **Kevin** = 3, **Joe** = 1.

Work done in 1st day (all three) = 9 + 3 + 1 = 13 units. Remaining = 14 units.

Since Kevin left 2 days before completion, Joe worked alone for those last 2 days: 2 × 1 = 2 units.

Work left for Kevin and Joe together = 14 − 2 = 12 units. Time taken = 12 ÷ (3 + 1) = 3 days.

Total days = 1 (together) + 3 (Kevin & Joe) + 2 (Joe alone) = 6 days.

**Formula Used:** Total Work = Time × Efficiency

 **Person** **Days** **Total Work** **Efficiency**
 **Ramesh** 16 80 5
 **Suresh** 10 8
**Calculations:**

⇒ Let the total work be completed in **x days**.

⇒ **Ramesh** worked for (x − 4) days and **Suresh** worked for x days.

⇒ Work done by **Ramesh** + Work done by **Suresh** = 80

⇒ 5 × (x − 4) + 8 × x = 80

⇒ 5x − 20 + 8x = 80

⇒ 13x = 100

⇒ x = 100/13 = 7(9/13) days

**∴ The correct answer is 7(9/13) days.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Leaving Early vs Joining Late

If a person leaves **'n' days before completion**, add (n × efficiency) to total work. If a person joins **'n' days late**, it does not change the total work units but reduces their active time.

Pipes and Cisterns

Similar logic applies where efficiency of an **outlet pipe** is taken as negative, while an **inlet pipe** is positive.

Work and Wages

Wages are always distributed in the ratio of the **actual work done** by each individual (Efficiency × Time).</p

questions.question: A and B can do a piece of work in 12 days and 18 days, respectively. Both work for 2 days and then A goes away and B completed the remaining work alone. The whole work was completed in ______________ days.
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Total Work (LCM of 12, 18) = 36 units.

Efficiency: A = 3, B = 2.

Combined work for 2 days = (3 + 2) × 2 = 10 units.

Remaining work = 36 − 10 = 26 units.

Time taken by B for remaining work = 26 ÷ 2 = 13 days.

Total time = 2 + 13 = 15 days.

**∴ The correct answer is 15 days.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Time taken by **A** = 12 days, Time taken by **B** = 18 days. Both work for 2 days.

 
 **Person** **Days** **Total Work** **Efficiency** 
 **A** 12 36 3 
 **B** 18 2 

⇒ **Total Work** = LCM(12, 18) = 36 units

⇒ **Efficiency** of A = 36 ÷ 12 = 3 units/day

⇒ **Efficiency** of B = 36 ÷ 18 = 2 units/day

⇒ Work done by **A and B** in 2 days = (3 + 2) × 2 = 10 units

⇒ **Remaining Work** = 36 − 10 = 26 units

⇒ Time taken by **B alone** to finish remaining work = 26 ÷ 2 = 13 days

⇒ **Total time** taken to complete the work = 2 + 13 = 15 days

**∴ The correct answer is 15 days.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Total Work Concept

Total work is usually considered as the **LCM** of the time taken by individuals to simplify efficiency calculations.

Work and Efficiency Relation

Efficiency is **inversely proportional** to the time taken. Efficiency = Total Work ÷ Time.

Leaving Work Logic

If a person leaves, subtract the work done before leaving from the **total work** and divide the remaining work by the efficiency of the remaining person.</p

questions.question: 13 men and 3 women can complete a piece of work in 7 days, and 5 men and 6 women can complete the same work in 18 days. The work of how many women is equivalent to that of one man?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Equate the **Total Work**: (13M + 3W) × 7 = (5M + 6W) × 18

91M + 21W = 90M + 108W

91M − 90M = 108W − 21W

1M = 87W

**∴ The correct answer is 87 women.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Case 1: **13 men** and **3 women** in **7 days**.

Case 2: **5 men** and **6 women** in **18 days**.

**Formula Used:**

Total Work = Efficiency × Time

**Calculations:**

Let the efficiency of one man be **M** and one woman be **W**.

⇒ Total Work = (13M + 3W) × 7

⇒ Total Work = (5M + 6W) × 18

⇒ 7(13M + 3W) = 18(5M + 6W)

⇒ 91M + 21W = 90M + 108W

⇒ 91M − 90M = 108W − 21W

⇒ 1M = 87W

⇒ Therefore, the work of 1 man is equivalent to 87 women.

**∴ The correct answer is 87 women.**

**__Additional Information__**

Work Equivalence Principle

When multiple groups perform the same work, we equate the product of their total efficiency and time: M₁D₁ = M₂D₂.

Efficiency Ratio

The ratio of the efficiency of a man to a woman is inversely proportional to the number of people required to do the same work.</p
